/-!
# Erdős Problem 303

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/303](https://www.erdosproblems.com/303)
- [BrRo91] Brown, Tom C. and Rödl, Voijtech, Monochromatic solutions to equations with unit
  fractions. Bull. Austral. Math. Soc. (1991), 387-392.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos303

/--
Is it true that in any finite colouring of the integers there exists a monochromatic solution
to $\frac 1 a = \frac 1 b + \frac 1 c$ with distinct $a, b, c$?

This is true, as proved by Brown and Rödl [BrRo91].

This was formalized in Lean by Yuan using Seed-Prover.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/303"]
theorem erdos_303 :
    answer(True) ↔
    -- For any finite colouring of the integers
    ∀ (𝓒 : ℤ → ℤ), (Set.range 𝓒).Finite →
      -- There exists integers `a, b, c`
      ∃ (a b c : ℤ),
      -- that are non-zero and distinct.
      [a, b, c, 0].Nodup ∧
      -- `a, b, c` satisfy the equation
      (1/a : ℝ) = 1/b + 1/c ∧
      -- `a, b, c` have the same color
      (𝓒 '' {a, b, c}).Subsingleton := by
  sorry

end Erdos303

reformulations.difference: The cited Brown–Rödl result uses positive integers, whereas Lean permits arbitrary nonzero integers as denominators. This agrees literally with the Erdős webpage's wording and is also equivalent to the positive-integer formulation.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The positive-integer assertion implies the integer assertion by restricting any colouring to positive integers. Conversely, for a positive-integer colouring C, colour each nonzero integer z by the pair (C(|z|), sign(z)), assigning zero an arbitrary colour. This is a finite colouring, encodable by integer labels. Any monochromatic nonzero triple then has a common sign. Taking absolute values preserves distinctness, its original colour, and the reciprocal equation, yielding a positive triple. In scratch Lean, zclaim_iff_positive proves the equivalence with requiring positive witnesses; zclaim_iff_finPalette separately verifies the finite-palette encoding. Neither proof depends on sorryAx.
